summary: Describes a backward-compatible technique for OSPF routers to advertise that they should not carry transit traffic, or that paths through them are less preferred. It was replaced by RFC 6987.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3137 describes how an OSPF router can ask other routers not to use it to reach other networks while keeping the router's own addresses reachable. It does this by advertising very high costs for links to other routers; RFC 6987 later replaced this informational memo.

questions: how to drain traffic from an ospf router
what is lsinf infinity in ospf
how can an ospf router avoid transit traffic
does an ospf stub router remain reachable
subtitle: A technique for making OSPF routers less attractive as transit paths.

tldr.problem: An OSPF router may need to stop carrying transit traffic while remaining reachable at its own addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The router advertises LSInfinity cost for non-stub links while retaining normal costs for stub links, encouraging other routers to choose alternate paths.

today: RFC 3137 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 6987.

sections.title: Remain Reachable Without Carrying Transit
sections.content:
A router can be in a critical condition, be introduced or removed gradually, or need to avoid transit traffic for administrative or traffic-engineering reasons. Simply removing its router-LSA would also prevent other routers from using paths to the router's own IP addresses.

The proposed approach keeps the router in the topology but advertises it as a stub for transit purposes. The memo notes that routing around it provides real benefits when the network has redundant paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can stay reachable while asking the network not to send other people's traffic through it. This helps when alternate paths exist.

sections.title: Advertising High Costs for Transit Links
sections.content: The router advertising itself as a stub sets costs for all non-stub links to LSInfinity, the 16-bit value 0xFFFF. It leaves the costs of stub links at their interface output costs. Other routers can then still reach prefixes directly connected to it while preferring paths that do not use it for transit.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps ordinary costs for its own directly connected networks and advertises an extremely high cost for links to other routers. Other routers can still reach its networks but prefer another route for transit.

sections.title: Behavior with Different OSPF Routers
sections.content:
The memo describes a difference between older OSPF calculations: implementations following RFC 1247 discard links with LSInfinity cost, while those following RFC 1583 and later do not treat them as unreachable. If alternate paths exist, both types prefer those paths over the one through the stub router. If the stub router is the only path, the older type avoids it and the newer type may still use it.

The memo says this inconsistency does not cause routing loops. It also states that the technique introduces no new OSPF security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Different OSPF versions may treat an infinite-cost link differently when it is the only route. When another path exists, both prefer that path, and the RFC says this does not create routing loops.

references.text: Moy, J., "OSPF Version 2", STD 54, RFC 2328, April 1998.
